newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mobutu envoy says Mandela agrees Zaire peace role.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu envoy says Mandela agrees Zaire peace role.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela has promised to play a major diplomatic role in peace efforts in central Africa, a senior Zairean envoy said on Thursday.
It was not clear what Mandela would do to help end fighting in the Great Lakes region, where Zaire's army has been battling ethnic Tutsi rebels supported by Rwanda.

"(Zairean) President Mobutu has asked his colleague (Mandela) to play a major diplomatic role in this conflict...and he is going to play the role that is expected from him in the situation that is occurring in Zaire," special envoy Honore Ngbanda told a news conference a day after talks with Mandela.
Ngbanda, special security adviser to Mobutu Sese Seko, said Mandela's government had also promised humanitarian assistance to the people in eastern Zaire.

Mandela has so far resisted a unilateral diplomatic role in peacemaking or a military role for his country's defence force, which is still merging the old apartheid army with members of the former liberation movements.
Senior African statesman Julius Nyerere, a former Tanzanian president, is expected to arrive on Saturday for talks with Mandela on the country's role in peace efforts.
Analysts said it was possible Mandela would try to arrange a meeting of regional leaders, including Nyerere and possibly Zimbabwe's Robert Mugabe, to thrash out issues confronting the region.

The Pretoria government on Wednesday suspended arms sales to Rwanda and said it would contribute to an international force for Zaire if asked by the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity.
East and Central African leaders called earlier this week for a neutral force to oversee the passage of aid to over a million refugees, mainly Rwandan Hutus, in eastern Zaire.
Prospects for an intervention force were boosted after an all-clear from ailing Mobutu, who said in France on Wednesday he backed the initiative.
But the Tutsi rebels known as Banyamulenge, who have implemented a unilateral ceasefire, oppose the deployment of a foreign force.
